To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the production of IFN-γ by antigen-specific T cells in atopy is diminished.

the production of interferon gamma by T cell lines specific for a purified protein derivative or a house dust mite allergen was diminished in patients with atopic dermatitis compared with healthy controls.
the production of IFN-γ by T cells specific to bacterial antigens was diminished in atopic patients compared with healthy controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of T cell‐mediated immunoregulation of atopy.
the mechanisms of Th2‐type responses in atopic patients, which are not limited to allergens, as well as the regulatory mechanisms of IFN‐gamma production by PPD‐reactive T cells in atopy.
the mechanism by which the Th2 response is skewed in atopic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

atopic patients have a Th2‐type response to both bacterial and allergen antigens, while healthy non‐atopic individuals have a Th1‐type response to the bacterial antigen, but the Th2‐response to the allergen.
the diminished IFN‐γ response by antigen‐stimulated T cells in atopy may be a result of a regulatory mechanism(s) rather than an intrinsic defect in T cells.
the diminished IFN‐γ secretion by PPD‐stimulated T cells from atopy patients is due to the Th2 cytokine‐mediated regulatory mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Th1/Th2‐type cytokine balance is skewed to the Th2 type in atopic patients.
the skewing of the Th1‐type T cell responses to the Th2 type may be one of the factors that contribute to the susceptibility of atopic patients to infections.

the Th2‐skewed cytokine production by antigen‐specific T lymphocytes is a characteristic of the allergic state, which is not restricted to the response to allergens but is also seen in the response to non‐allergic antigens such as PPD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
atopic individuals have a reduced production of IFN-γ by PPD-specific T cells, and this is not due to intrinsic T cell defect, but to some regulatory mechanism.

the skewing of T cell cytokine responses in atopic patients occurs not only with allergen‐specific T cells but also with T cells specific for bacterial antigens, such as PPD, compared with nonatopic individuals.
the skewing of T‐cell response in atopic individuals is not only a response to allergens but also a response to bacterial antigens.
